description: We are Space Syntax, engineering students from El Salvador (software, mechatronics and robotics). We love tech, games and space. Skills: full-stack web, UI/UX, data visualization, AI and robotics. Looking for teammates into coding, game design or space science.
summary: Is the Moon made of cheese? In How Far Is Up?, that question becomes a mission you get to design. Team Space Syntax built an educational browser game where teens use NASA and ESA resources to plan a lunar mission, make engineering trade-offs, and gather evidence. Players choose what to investigate, build a spacecraft, test their plan, and explore the Moon. At the end, the evidence they collected determines what they can conclude.
details:
We built How Far Is Up? to give teens a chance to turn a question into a test and make decisions with limited resources. The game starts with a familiar idea that the Moon might be made of cheese and puts the player in charge of finding out.

Design the mission. Choose a question, select instruments, build a spacecraft, and pick a rocket. For a crewed mission, adding people or days changes how much oxygen, food, and water you need to carry.

Test the plan and launch. Plan the engine burns, set a fuel reserve, and test the communications link with a simulated ping. See how your choices affect mass, power, and budget.

Land and investigate. Compare landing sites and start the descent. If rocks appear, decide whether to spend part of your reserve on a detour or abort. On the surface, your instruments determine whether you can photograph the terrain, measure composition, or collect a sample.

Review the evidence. A return mission adds choices about reentry and the heat shield. A one-way robotic mission sends findings to Earth. In the lab, a photo can offer a clue, while a composition reading or a sample can support a stronger conclusion.

We built the interface in React and the simulation engine in JavaScript. Players can explore the math and open source links inside the game. Parameters chosen for gameplay appear as game values.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

We used AI tools as a support throughout the project. All final decisions, game design and code review were made by the team.

  • Research: AI assistants helped us find and summarize official NASA and ESA sources. We checked each value against its original link, and every source used in the game can be opened from inside it.(Grokbot)
  • Design: We used AI to brainstorm screen layouts, mini-game ideas and the pitch deck structure, then picked and adapted what fit our story.(OpenAI and Grokbot)
  • Development: We used AI coding assistants (Claude) for code suggestions, the move from plain JavaScript to React, and writing tests for the simulation engine.
  • Debugging: AI helped us find, explain and fix errors during development.(Claude)
